properties.digitization_method: REDONE 2026-09-14: the diagram-transform version of this polygon (described below, kept for history) placed Building 2 entirely on the paved road median of Illinois St -- confirmed wrong against satellite imagery (no structure there at all). User pointed out the real match is not the warehouse building across the street, but the large vacant/graded lot on the WEST side of Illinois St, between roughly 20th and 21st St -- its silhouette (elongated, tilted a few degrees off true north, matching the local curb bearing) is the same shape being traced, just larger. Re-traced directly from that lot's own visible boundary: anchored on two points read off the lot's real east edge (the Illinois St curb, high-contrast and unambiguous), which gave a measured bearing of ~182.3/272.3 degrees. CORRECTED same day: user caught that this made the east edge visibly non-parallel to the real curb -- the two curb points used for that bearing were only ~13m apart (an 80m along-curb baseline but just ~3.5m of east-west offset between them), so a 1-2 pixel misreading at zoom 20 (~0.3-0.6m each) was enough to swing the derived bearing by several degrees -- exactly the 'reading points too close together, small errors don't cancel' failure this project's bearing_trace.py already warns about, repeated instead of heeded. Fixed by using this site's already-established, multiply-validated grid bearing (176.5/356.5 degrees, from Historic Building 14's real surveyed footprint, and consistent with Block B's own independently-confirmed ~175 degrees) instead of re-deriving a fresh one from a short noisy baseline; kept the same real anchor point and the same independently-measured distances (~126m north-south, ~51m east-west). SECOND CORRECTION, same day: user caught that the resulting rectangle still overlapped the street -- the anchor point itself (read near a crosswalk with parked cars and shadow clutter) was actually ~8-9m INSIDE the road, not on the curb, even though the bearing was by then correct. Root cause: misread the sidewalk/asphalt color transition in a cluttered spot. Re-read the curb at two clean, unobstructed points well clear of any crosswalk (via a brightness-transition scan of the sidewalk-to-asphalt boundary at zoom 20, cross-checked against the pixel-to-lonlat math directly rather than by eye), which independently reproduced the same 176.57 degree bearing (confirming the established bearing was never the problem) but placed the curb about 8.5m further west than the previous anchor. Extrapolated the corrected curb line to the same north/south extents and rebuilt the west edge at the same 51m width. Overlay-checked both the north and south corners individually afterward: the east edge now sat on the sidewalk side of the curb along its whole length, not on the asphalt. THIRD CORRECTION, same day: user pointed out the east edge was still at the OUTER (curb) side of the public Illinois St sidewalk, meaning the polygon's area included the whole ~4.5m-wide public sidewalk itself, not just the private lot -- and that the south edge (the cross-street's own sidewalk/crosswalk) had the identical problem, cutting straight through the crosswalk stripe pattern rather than stopping at the back of that sidewalk. Fixed both: re-read the INNER (lot-side/back-of-sidewalk) edge of the Illinois St sidewalk, at the dirt-to-concrete color transition on the lot side rather than the concrete-to-asphalt transition on the street side (found ~4.5m west of the previous curb-line anchor, at the same validated 176.5 degree bearing -- confirms this project's east edges up to now, including PKN/PKS/E1/E2/HDY3 etc., were anchored on curbs; worth re-checking whether any of those also failed to exclude a real sidewalk). Re-read the south edge similarly: found the true back-of-sidewalk transition on the lot side of the cross-street's own sidewalk (north of its crosswalk stripes, not through them) and rebuilt the south edge through that point, perpendicular to the same established bearing, solving for new SE/SW corners as the intersection with the (unchanged) east and west edge lines. Overlay-confirmed the south edge now runs clear of the crosswalk stripes along its whole length. FOURTH CORRECTION (negligible, ~0.17m): when generalizing this fix into a reusable, tested function (bearing_trace.rectangle_from_four_edges, added along with src/test_bearing_trace.py), recomputing NE from the same raw measured anchors gave a corner ~0.17m from the hand-computed one above (accumulated rounding across several manual correction passes) -- adjusted NE to match the function's output exactly, so the file and the tested reconstruction agree bit-for-bit rather than by coincidence. See src/test_bearing_trace.py for the from-scratch reconstruction this geometry must continue to match. NOTE: this lot is visibly larger (~126m x 51m) than Warehouse No. 2's documented 236ft x 76ft (~72m x 23m) footprint, and satellite imagery shows no internal boundary, fence, or foundation distinguishing a smaller building footprint within it -- the lot currently reads as a single, undivided vacant/graded surface, which is actually consistent with this file's own (previously contradictory) accuracy_caveat text describing 'vacant/graded land,' despite regulatory_context describing Warehouse No. 2 as an existing historic structure. This polygon is therefore the best satellite-confirmable placeholder (the real, shared lot the building's documented footprint sits within) but is NOT a precise building footprint -- treat it as an upper bound on Building 2's true location, not the building's actual extent, and treat the 'historic structure, existing' status in this file with caution pending a source that resolves the discrepancy. Overlaps Parcels C1 and C2 (860 m2 and 1035 m2) in this project's own overlap QA -- not clipped, because all three are approximate placeholders competing for the same currently-undivided vacant lot; clipping any of them against another would not make any of them more accurate. See C1/C2's own accuracy_caveat for the matching note. Prior diagram-transform method (for history): traced from the Pier 70 Design for Development's own Figure 6.4.2 (Maximum Building Height, p.155) -- an adopted regulatory diagram with a printed scale bar, north arrow, and real street labels, not an illustrative rendering. Georeferenced using 5 real street-intersection control points (Illinois St and Michigan St, each crossing 20th St and 21st St) fetched from OpenStreetMap via this project's own src/fetch_streets.py, plus the real, independently-confirmed position of Historic Building 12 (blklot 4114010) as a 6th anchor, fit as a least-squares affine transform. Residual error against the fitted control points is roughly 8-25m -- wider than Mission Rock's equivalent transform (which had more, better-distributed real street intersections available). RELOCATED 2026-09-16 (full Pier 70 geometry restart): the west-lot placement above is WRONG, not just imprecise. Root cause: this project's own D4D research had already surfaced that Building 21's sourcing describes 'the historic node of Buildings 2, 12, and 21' (Figure 3.6.1's caption) -- i.e. Building 2 should sit immediately next to the real, confirmed positions of Building 12 (blklot 4114010) and Building 21 (re-traced 2026-09-16), on the EAST side of the site near Maryland St. It does not; Figure 6.4.2 itself confirms this directly, showing a gray 'Historic Building' box labeled plainly '2' immediately next to the 'D' and '12' boxes in that same east cluster -- not anywhere near Illinois St/C1/C2 where the west-lot version was placed. The west-lot placement was a guess made without checking this: it was chosen only because it was the nearest large satellite-visible vacant/graded surface west of Illinois St, without cross-referencing the diagram's own explicit label placement for '2', and without noticing that a 126m x 51m 'whole shared lot' was already flagged in this very file as 4x larger than Warehouse No. 2's documented 236ft x 76ft footprint -- a mismatch that should have been the tell. Re-traced this block's real position directly: isolated the gray 'Historic Building' legend color (RGB [148,150,153]) in the east cluster, extracted a clean rectangular contour (OpenCV) at pixel (1140,737)-(1206,961), and converted via the same validated 6-point affine transform used for Building 21 and the numbered parcels. Resulting area (~15,235 sqft) is a close match (85%) to the documented 236ft x 76ft (~17,936 sqft) footprint -- strong independent confirmation this is the right building, unlike the west-lot version's 4x-oversized mismatch. Confirmed zero overlap with Building 21, Parcel D, or Building 12 Plaza. The former west-lot placement's own extensive correction history (five passes, all satellite-based) is kept below for the record, but none of that work applies to this building's real position -- it was carefully refining the wrong location.

properties.digitized_from: Potrero Power Station Design for Development, Figure 6.2.3 - Building Height Plan (p.245).
properties.digitization_method: Traced from the Potrero Power Station Design for Development's own Figure 6.2.3 (Building Height Plan, p.245) -- an adopted regulatory diagram with a printed scale bar, north arrow, and real street labels (Illinois St, Georgia St, Louisiana St, Maryland St, Delaware St, 22nd St, Humboldt St, 23rd St), not an illustrative rendering. Georeferenced using 9 real street-intersection control points fetched from OpenStreetMap via this project's own src/fetch_streets.py, fit as a least-squares affine transform. NOTE: an initial attempt also used the real, confirmed positions of the Sophie Maxwell Building and the UCSF Block 2 building as anchors, but they produced 50-60m of error against the street-only fit -- this diagram is dated Feb 26, 2020, predating UCSF's ~2023-24 arrival as a life-science anchor tenant, so those two real buildings likely do not sit where this 2020 figure's own numbered blocks would place them (their own real parcels are used directly elsewhere in this dataset and were NOT re-derived from this diagram). The final transform here uses street intersections only. Residual error against those control points is roughly 8-24m. Traced polygons were additionally clipped against the real, confirmed Sophie Maxwell and UCSF Block 2 parcels (and against Prequel Park's approximate geometry) so this speculative tracing never overrides real or better-sourced geometry. CORRECTED 2026-09-16: user-flagged pattern of blocks encroaching on real streets across the site (Block 3, Block 11, Block 12) led to rebuilding this whole block layer from scratch using proper GCP-based georeferencing (GDAL's gdaltransform with a thin-plate-spline transform, the same technique QGIS's Georeferencer uses) instead of patching individual curbs. Installed GDAL, computed 8 real street-intersection ground control points from OpenStreetMap data (Craig Lane x Maryland St, 22nd St x Maryland/Louisiana St, Humboldt St x Maryland/Delaware/Georgia Lane, 23rd St x Maryland/Georgia Lane), precisely located each in the source diagram (Figure 6.2.3) via programmatic black-pixel border detection cross-checked with visual ruler crops, and fit a TPS transform. Re-traced this block's own corner pixels the same way and ran them through the new transform. This corrected transform disagrees with the original 9-point affine transform by tens of meters in places -- e.g. it revealed the original trace had Blocks 3/4 shifted east into the excavation pit/street area, and Blocks 11/12 roughly 2x too deep -- and the new positions now land within real, distinct site features (buildings, graded lots) visible in satellite imagery rather than straddling roads. Known residual limitation: GCP street positions are centerline-based (matching OSM convention), while a block boundary should sit at the near curb, so any edge close to a GCP street can land a few meters into that street after transformation -- checked for and corrected on this block's street-facing edge(s) where applicable using this project's already-established grid bearing (356.5 deg) and, where available, an independently diagram-measured depth/width. Treat corrected vertex positions as accurate to roughly 10-15m (tighter than the original 8-24m transform, but still not survey-grade). RE-CORRECTED 2026-09-16 (same day, third pass): the independent per-block TPS re-trace (see above) still measured each block's own 4 corners in isolation, which -- despite using the same transform -- left small (3-12m) spurious gaps or misalignments at boundaries the diagram actually draws as shared or tightly-spaced between adjacent blocks (caught after the user pointed out the diagram itself has ~zero wasted space and specifically that the PG&E switchyard polygon sits directly against Block 5 in the diagram, not ~60m away as this dataset had it). Re-measured EVERY block's corners in a single consistent pass using programmatic black-pixel border detection (long contiguous runs = real borders, filtered from text/dimension-arrow strokes by requiring the run to span nearly the full block height/width), cross-validated with fine-pixel-gridline crops, so that shared or consistently-measured boundaries between neighboring blocks now come from the same underlying pixel measurements rather than independent eyeball estimates. Batch-transformed through the same GDAL/TPS fit as before. This pass also corrected several block extents that were measured imprecisely in the prior pass (e.g. Block 5's real stepped/notched south edge, Block 11's true position -- it does NOT sit flush against Block 15, there is real Power Station Park open space between them). GCP CORRECTION 2026-09-16 (fourth pass): user flagged that Block 8/12 should touch Delaware Street with park space between them, and that Block 3/4's shapes looked off -- investigation found the root cause was a single mis-measured ground control point. The 'Delaware St x Humboldt St' GCP used for the whole site's TPS transform had been placed at pixel (2227, 986), which is actually deep inside Building 9's own footprint in the diagram, not on Delaware Street at all -- confirmed by comparing pixel spacing between the three Humboldt-row GCPs (Maryland/Delaware/Georgia Lane): Maryland-to-Georgia-Lane's pixel:real-world ratio implied Delaware should sit at roughly pixel x=2020, not 2227, and a direct color-transition scan at y=986 confirmed the real street gap is at x=1994-2035. Corrected the GCP to (2015, 986) (same real-world coordinate, just the right pixel) and re-ran the TPS transform for the whole site. This produced large corrections concentrated exactly where the user's complaint pointed -- Block 4 shifted 33-60m, Block 3's east corners ~28-33m, Block 8's east corners ~29-31m, Block 12's east corners ~26-27m -- while blocks far from the error (5, 15, 7, 11, PG&E) shifted well under 5m, consistent with a localized GCP error rather than a global transform problem.

properties.digitization_method: Traced from the Potrero Power Station Design for Development's own Figure 6.2.3 (Building Height Plan, p.245) -- an adopted regulatory diagram with a printed scale bar, north arrow, and real street labels (Illinois St, Georgia St, Louisiana St, Maryland St, Delaware St, 22nd St, Humboldt St, 23rd St), not an illustrative rendering. Georeferenced using 9 real street-intersection control points fetched from OpenStreetMap via this project's own src/fetch_streets.py, fit as a least-squares affine transform. NOTE: an initial attempt also used the real, confirmed positions of the Sophie Maxwell Building and the UCSF Block 2 building as anchors, but they produced 50-60m of error against the street-only fit -- this diagram is dated Feb 26, 2020, predating UCSF's ~2023-24 arrival as a life-science anchor tenant, so those two real buildings likely do not sit where this 2020 figure's own numbered blocks would place them (their own real parcels are used directly elsewhere in this dataset and were NOT re-derived from this diagram). The final transform here uses street intersections only. Residual error against those control points is roughly 8-24m. Traced polygons were additionally clipped against the real, confirmed Sophie Maxwell and UCSF Block 2 parcels (and against Prequel Park's approximate geometry) so this speculative tracing never overrides real or better-sourced geometry. CORRECTED 2026-09-16: user-flagged pattern of blocks encroaching on real streets across the site (Block 3, Block 11, Block 12) led to rebuilding this whole block layer from scratch using proper GCP-based georeferencing (GDAL's gdaltransform with a thin-plate-spline transform, the same technique QGIS's Georeferencer uses) instead of patching individual curbs. Installed GDAL, computed 8 real street-intersection ground control points from OpenStreetMap data (Craig Lane x Maryland St, 22nd St x Maryland/Louisiana St, Humboldt St x Maryland/Delaware/Georgia Lane, 23rd St x Maryland/Georgia Lane), precisely located each in the source diagram (Figure 6.2.3) via programmatic black-pixel border detection cross-checked with visual ruler crops, and fit a TPS transform. Re-traced this block's own corner pixels the same way and ran them through the new transform. This corrected transform disagrees with the original 9-point affine transform by tens of meters in places -- e.g. it revealed the original trace had Blocks 3/4 shifted east into the excavation pit/street area, and Blocks 11/12 roughly 2x too deep -- and the new positions now land within real, distinct site features (buildings, graded lots) visible in satellite imagery rather than straddling roads. Known residual limitation: GCP street positions are centerline-based (matching OSM convention), while a block boundary should sit at the near curb, so any edge close to a GCP street can land a few meters into that street after transformation -- checked for and corrected on this block's street-facing edge(s) where applicable using this project's already-established grid bearing (356.5 deg) and, where available, an independently diagram-measured depth/width. Treat corrected vertex positions as accurate to roughly 10-15m (tighter than the original 8-24m transform, but still not survey-grade). RE-CORRECTED 2026-09-16 (same day, third pass): the independent per-block TPS re-trace (see above) still measured each block's own 4 corners in isolation, which -- despite using the same transform -- left small (3-12m) spurious gaps or misalignments at boundaries the diagram actually draws as shared or tightly-spaced between adjacent blocks (caught after the user pointed out the diagram itself has ~zero wasted space and specifically that the PG&E switchyard polygon sits directly against Block 5 in the diagram, not ~60m away as this dataset had it). Re-measured EVERY block's corners in a single consistent pass using programmatic black-pixel border detection (long contiguous runs = real borders, filtered from text/dimension-arrow strokes by requiring the run to span nearly the full block height/width), cross-validated with fine-pixel-gridline crops, so that shared or consistently-measured boundaries between neighboring blocks now come from the same underlying pixel measurements rather than independent eyeball estimates. Batch-transformed through the same GDAL/TPS fit as before. This pass also corrected several block extents that were measured imprecisely in the prior pass (e.g. Block 5's real stepped/notched south edge, Block 11's true position -- it does NOT sit flush against Block 15, there is real Power Station Park open space between them). GCP CORRECTION 2026-09-16 (fourth pass): user flagged that Block 8/12 should touch Delaware Street with park space between them, and that Block 3/4's shapes looked off -- investigation found the root cause was a single mis-measured ground control point. The 'Delaware St x Humboldt St' GCP used for the whole site's TPS transform had been placed at pixel (2227, 986), which is actually deep inside Building 9's own footprint in the diagram, not on Delaware Street at all -- confirmed by comparing pixel spacing between the three Humboldt-row GCPs (Maryland/Delaware/Georgia Lane): Maryland-to-Georgia-Lane's pixel:real-world ratio implied Delaware should sit at roughly pixel x=2020, not 2227, and a direct color-transition scan at y=986 confirmed the real street gap is at x=1994-2035. Corrected the GCP to (2015, 986) (same real-world coordinate, just the right pixel) and re-ran the TPS transform for the whole site. This produced large corrections concentrated exactly where the user's complaint pointed -- Block 4 shifted 33-60m, Block 3's east corners ~28-33m, Block 8's east corners ~29-31m, Block 12's east corners ~26-27m -- while blocks far from the error (5, 15, 7, 11, PG&E) shifted well under 5m, consistent with a localized GCP error rather than a global transform problem.

On closer inspection this reading fits the image better: the elongated shape has a consistent width along its whole length, a distinct rounded rim at its far (south) end matching a flue opening now lying at grade, and no consistent shadow offset you'd expect from a true parallax lean. properties.project_name: Mission Creek Park South Extension -- P8 segment
properties.digitized_from: Hand-traced from satellite imagery (contextily/Esri World Imagery) against the currently-visible graded/disturbed extent, cross-checked against SF Recreation & Parks' own Mission Creek Park South Extension Project page and its Schematic Design document (P2 and P8, Feb 2022 CAC materials). UPDATED 2026-09-20: extended via a numbered real-gap-fragment technique -- bbox.difference(street buffer, src/street_geometry.py).difference(all already-tracked parcels/approx polygons) over the Mission Bay Circle roundabout area yielded ~68 disconnected candidate scraps of unclaimed real land; the owner picked a specific union by index while viewing a numbered map of all of them (fragments 4, 17, 34, 41, 18), a technique the owner asked to reuse for future ambiguous boundaries.
properties.digitization_method: ADDED 2026-09-19 as 'P2 (meadow/community garden segment)' -- owner named this as a real, funded project while reviewing a zoomed map+drawing pair, researched and confirmed via SF Recreation & Parks' own project page (sfrecpark.org/1833) and schematic-design PDF (sfrecpark.org/DocumentCenter/View/25950). RELABELED 2026-09-20: this specific traced polygon is actually the P8 parcel, not P2 -- the owner clarified the overall scheme once P1 (data/manual/mission_bay_creek_park_p1_p3.geojson), P9 and P7 were resolved: P2 is the prolongation of P1 southwest along the creek, down to about where this polygon starts, and P8 takes over from there down toward the Mission Bay Circle roundabout (P9/P7 continue further south again). This polygon sits in that P8 stretch, immediately south of the already-tracked real 'Mission Creek Park' record's own south tip and north of P9/P7 -- not in the P2 stretch, which for now has no separate traced geometry of its own (see docs/briefs/mission_bay_block_inventory.csv's P2 row). The underlying trace, sourcing and street-buffer trim are otherwise unchanged from the original 2026-09-19 pass: traced against the visible graded/disturbed extent east of the I-280 viaduct, trimmed against src/street_geometry.py's real street buffer (22% of the raw hand-trace fell inside it), kept the largest resulting piece and simplified it (shapely simplify, tolerance 0.00001 deg). EXTENDED 2026-09-20: the owner, reviewing a wide real-street reference map with the already-traced P1 and the prior small P8 polygon shown for context, drew where P2 and P8 should actually run (P2 as the P1-to-roundabout prolongation along the creek/Channel St corridor, P8 taking over from the roundabout south/east under the freeway toward Berry St). For P8's freeway-interchange stretch, rather than trace the owner's freehand line directly, generated a numbered map of every disconnected real (street-buffer- and already-tracked-polygon-excluded) scrap of land in the area (68 candidates) and had the owner pick the exact union by index: the existing polygon above plus fragments 4, 17, 34, 41 and 18. Two follow-up trims per the owner: (1) fragment 18 is a ribbon-and-blob shape running along the west side of the interchange next to the Channel Pump Station (X1) -- found the natural waist of the ribbon by scanning cross-sectional width along its length (narrows to ~1.6m at lat 37.77020 before widening into the ~660 sqm south blob and separately into the north ribbon toward the creek) and cut there, keeping only the south blob per the owner's 'remove the thin ribbon going towards the creek'. (2) fragment 4 is a large, irregularly-shaped scrap whose own boundary already contains a straight diagonal edge (~52m + ~37m segments) exactly where it borders the interchange landscaping; fit a line through the north corners of fragments 34, 41 and 17 (all landscaped medians between freeway ramps that already terminate on that same real edge) -- the three points were colinear to within ~5e-8 deg, confirming it's one real physical edge, not three coincidences -- and confirmed fragment 4's own existing diagonal edge sits exactly on that same line. Cut fragment 4 along the extended line and kept the piece(s) on the fragments' own (south/east) side, which drops a ~2380 sqm lobe on the far side of that edge (matching the owner's 'so P8 north side aligns across all polygons: 34, 41, 17, truncated 4'). Verified against Esri World Imagery: the kept shape lands on real turf (the roundabout-side park lawn, and three landscaped median strips between the I-280 ramps on the west side of Owens St/the interchange), and the internal notches the fragment computation already carved out track real paved walkways crossing the lawn. Result is a MultiPolygon: the roundabout-side lawn (includes the original small polygon, now absorbed), three separate freeway-median strips (fragments 34/41/17, not touching each other -- real gaps between them), and the trimmed piece-18 blob next to the pump station.
properties.accuracy_caveat: APPROXIMATE -- real turf/median extent per Esri satellite imagery and the owner's own hand-drawn scheme (street/creek-bounded gap-fragment technique, not surveyed). The three freeway-median strips and the pump-station-side blob are deliberately kept as separate polygons in a MultiPolygon (they are physically separated by pavement/ramp lanes, not one contiguous parcel). Overlaps the already-tracked real 'Mission Creek Park' polygon for part of its northeast extent -- not reconciled with it yet, per the owner's own framing that Mission Creek Park will eventually evolve to encompass P1+P2+P8.
properties.notes: Mission Creek Park South Extension Project, P8 segment (see P2's row in the block inventory for the project's other parcel). Design principles per the schematic: respect the Mission Creek Harbor Association community, relocate/expand the existing community garden, add teaching and perennial gardens, meadow planting and native shrub berms partially under the freeway. Project manager: Monica Scott (SF Rec & Park), monica.scott@sfgov.org. Extended 2026-09-20 to the owner's fuller P8 scheme: the roundabout-side lawn plus the freeway-median strips and pump-station-side turf between the I-280 ramps, west of the roundabout.

properties.project_name: P2 -- open-space strip between Mission Creek and Channel St
properties.digitized_from: Real-gap-fragment technique: bbox.difference(street buffer, src/street_geometry.py)..difference(all already-tracked parcels/approx polygons) over the creek corridor between Mission Creek and Channel St yielded a numbered set of disconnected real scraps of unclaimed land; the owner, viewing the numbered map against Esri satellite imagery, picked fragment 7 (the paved/planted strip along the creek's near bank) and fragment 9 (a paved path further southeast, separated from 7 by a landscaping/tree strip not itself captured as its own fragment) and specified how to combine them.
properties.digitization_method: ADDED 2026-09-20 via the numbered real-gap-fragment technique established for P8 (see that record): generated a map of every disconnected real (street-buffer- and already-tracked-polygon-excluded) scrap of land in the creek/Channel St corridor between about where P8 hands off (near the roundabout) and the creek bend northeast of it. Two rounds of owner review (first pass, then a request to extend the view further northeast) converged on: fragment 7, truncated at its north edge along the same real line P8's fragment 4 was cut on (a line fit through the north corners of P8's fragments 34/41/17, confirmed colinear to ~5e-8 deg) -- at fragment 7's own longitude range this line lands almost exactly on its existing north boundary (matching to within ~0.00015 deg at the fragment's far corner), separating the real open water of Mission Creek (the ~9,854 sqm piece north of the line, discarded) from the real paved/planted strip along the near bank (~4,855 sqm, kept). The owner then specified translating fragment 9 (a separate paved path, ~7,932 sqm) north to merge with the truncated fragment 7, closing a real but narrow (~17-22m) planting-strip gap between the two rather than tracing that gap directly -- picked a 0.0002 deg (~22m) north shift, comfortably past the ~0.000156 deg (~17.3m) minimum needed for the two shapes to touch, for a clean overlapping seam rather than a knife-edge join. Final shape is the union of truncated-7 and shifted-9 (~12,224 sqm). PRE-CLIPPED 2026-09-20 against the real street buffer (src/street_geometry.py) before committing: the union (fragment 7 truncated + fragment 9 translated north) reached into a real paved area near the boat-dock access road at its northeast end -- join_approximate.py --strict flagged this as a 25% MAJOR CLIP, at the threshold where the checker asks for a direct look rather than trusting the auto-clip. Inspected directly against Esri satellite imagery: the removed area is a real paved road/driveway crossing plus the road-side verge, not a mispositioned trace, so committed the pre-clipped result (12,224 sqm -> 9,128 sqm) directly rather than relying on the pipeline's silent auto-clip every run. Splits into three pieces: the near-bank strip (4,977 sqm), the road-side strip that was fragment 9 (3,896 sqm), and a small separate grassy patch near the boat dock (255 sqm) that the clip revealed as disconnected from the other two. TRIMMED 2026-09-20: dropped the small (~255 sqm) disconnected triangle near the boat dock at P2's northeast end per the owner's review -- an artifact of the street clip, not real intended P2 open space. Final: 2 pieces, ~8,873 sqm. properties.project_name: SF Railyards -- Caltrain rail yard and 4th & King Station (Prologis/Caltrain redevelopment)
properties.digitized_from: Bounded by DataSF's official street centerlines (data/raw/official_street_centerlines.geojson): Townsend St (4th-7th) on the north, 4th St (Townsend-King) on the east, 7th St (Townsend-King) on the west, and King St (4th-~6th, where its real centerline data ends) on the south, each buffered by the project's standard measured half-width (src/street_geometry.py, 6.8m) and inset from the outer street-to-street ring by that same half-width to approximate the curb/yard edge rather than the street centerline itself -- same method as P9 (data/manual/mission_bay_p9_open_space.geojson). King St's real DataSF centerline stops short of 7th St (its last segment ends at -122.397986, 37.773324): that stretch of the site's real southern edge is not a city street at all but the I-280 northbound/southbound ramp interchange (confirmed both by the DataSF centerlines' own 'I-280 N/S ON/OFF RAMP' segments in the same file and by satellite imagery, which shows the ramp curving directly along the yard's southwest taper), so the closing edge there is a straight line from King St's last real point to 7th St's King-St corner, not a surveyed street. The resulting inset polygon is 20.08 acres, matching the SF Planning/Caltrain FAQ's own '20-acre site' description almost exactly, and its outline was checked directly against Esri World Imagery (via contextily) overlaid in QGIS-equivalent fashion -- it tracks the real fan of tracks and the 4th & King station platform canopy tightly, confirmed by the site owner 2026-09-21 after a side-by-side review of the overlay.
properties.accuracy_caveat: APPROXIMATE -- not a surveyed parcel or a GIS file from Caltrain/Prologis/SF Planning. The active rail right-of-way here carries no Assessor block/lot in DataSF's Parcels - Active and Retired dataset (checked directly; consistent with railroad right-of-way being outside the normal local assessment roll), so this could not be joined via status.csv like a real parcel. Three of the four sides (Townsend, 4th, 7th) are real, continuous DataSF street centerlines; the fourth (King St plus a straight closing line where King's real data ends short of 7th, at the I-280 interchange) is the weakest edge and the one most likely to need revision if a real project boundary or EIR figure becomes available. Includes the existing Caltrain 4th & King Street Station itself, which the project's own description treats as part of the site being redeveloped, not something outside it.
properties.notes: SF Planning Case No. 2023-000384CWP, 'SF Railyards Planning Program'. The 20-acre site at the nexus of SoMa, Mission Bay and Showplace Square: Caltrain's northern terminus and an active service/maintenance yard, owned by Prologis with Caltrain holding a perpetual easement to operate rail. A Development Agreement is the expected approval path (precedent: Pier 70, Mission Rock, Potrero Power Station, all DAs). Directly borders Mission Bay North: OCII's own December 2019 Mission Bay Land Use Map shows the blocks informally labeled N5A, N6 and N7 in this area with no assigned land use and no drawn boundary (unlike every neighboring numbered Mission Bay North block, which has both), consistent with this still being active rail infrastructure outside Mission Bay North's own planned build-out as of that map.
